title: Bath-time body words: eight bilingual words you can wash, splash and name
description: Bath time already happens every day, with a child who is not going anywhere. Eight body words, one simple washing game, and nothing to buy or print.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: Bath-time body words: eight bilingual words you can wash, splash and name
body:
Bath time has two things most vocabulary practice lacks: it happens every day, and your child is not going anywhere. That makes it a good slot for a small set of words you repeat — and body parts are the easiest set to start with, because your child can see and touch every one of them.

Choose eight words. A good first set: hands, feet, knees, neck, nose, ears, hair, back. In Spanish: las manos, los pies, las rodillas, el cuello, la nariz, las orejas, el pelo, la espalda. Whenever Spanish is in play, say the article with the noun every time, so it comes attached to the word.

The game is simply "wash the…". Say only the word, in the language you are building, and your child washes whatever you named. If you are building Spanish: "¡los pies!" and the feet get scrubbed. If you are building English: "knees!" and the knees get scrubbed. No translation needed — the action shows you whether the word landed. When you want a full sentence, the pattern is "Lávate las manos" or "wash your hands".

Round two, swap. Your child gives the orders and washes a bath toy's "feet" or "ears", or tells you which of your hands to wash. Children love giving instructions to an adult, and every instruction is a word said out loud.

Round three is the silly one: name the wrong part on purpose. Point to a knee and say "la nariz" — or "the nose". Most children correct you at once, and correcting you is a confident way to use a word.

Keep it inside a normal bath. Do not add minutes; the routine only survives if it costs nothing. The towel gives you one last round: dry the hands, the feet, the hair, naming each one as you go.

A few practical points. Stay with the same eight words for a week before swapping any. If your child answers in the other language, repeat the word in the language you are building and keep going — no correction needed. And on a tired, grumpy night, skip it. One skipped bath does not undo anything.

Next week, keep six words and swap in two new ones. Faces make a good second set: eyes, mouth, teeth, cheeks — los ojos, la boca, los dientes, las mejillas.
qa_checklist: A bilingual (EN/ES) reader checks both languages, not a tool
No claims about fluency, test scores or developmental outcomes
Every activity works with what is already in the house: no printer, no purchase
Original text written for this page, not lifted from the book
CTA is honest: a Kindle vocabulary book read on a screen, lists copied into a notebook
semantic_review: English body with single Spanish body-part nouns, always with their article. Scripts shown in both directions (¡los pies! / knees!, Lávate las manos / wash your hands). Regional words avoided (no word for bathtub or tummy).
claims_check: No outcome promises. The text says what to do and how long it takes; it does not claim fluency, school results or cognitive benefits.
